issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s death does not extinguish an eviction claim based on occupation for the landlord and members of the landlord’s family when those family members’ occupation is also a basis of the claim.
material_facts: The court considered a rule applied in an eviction proceeding where the landlord sought residential occupation for himself and members of his family and died while an appeal was pending.

The court held that the statutory wording made the need for occupation the need of both the landlord and the family members, and that family members could continue the proceeding through the senior member of the family.
issues.conclusion: The right to sue survives to the landlord’s family members where the claim is for occupation by the landlord and members of the family; the contrary holding in Phul Rani was overruled.
issues.legal_principle: The court interpreted section 14(1)(e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, which permitted eviction for occupation as a residence for the landlord and members of the landlord’s family. Because the provision included the family members’ occupation, their need did not cease on the landlord’s death. The court overruled Phul Rani & Ors. v. Naubat Rai Ahluwalia.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction of a tenant under rent-control law.
predicates.landlord_dies_while_claim_pending: The landlord dies while the eviction claim is still pending.
predicates.claimed_occupation_includes_family_membe: The claimed occupation is for the landlord and members of the landlord’s family.

issues.definition: When a rent-control eviction claim for occupation by the landlord and family members remains pending after the landlord dies, the family members can continue the claim.

issues.legal_issue: A family member who has no interest in a partnership cannot establish personal need for premises merely because the landlord’s claimed need is for the partnership’s use.
material_facts: The original landlord claimed that he reasonably and bona fide required the premises for a partnership in which he was a partner.
After his death, a new partnership was formed; two of his sons joined it, but his minor son was not admitted to its benefits and had no interest in it.
The premises were sought for the partnership’s storage and business use, which the court found could not be treated as the minor son’s requirement.
issues.conclusion: The minor son could not be said to require the premises because he had no interest in the partnership. The court did not decide whether a landlord’s requirement for a partnership in which the landlord is a partner otherwise amounts to the landlord’s own occupation.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 13(1)(g) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, the court assumed, without deciding, that a landlord’s requirement for a partnership’s use could be covered. It held that the heir who had no interest in the partnership could not be said to require the premises for himself.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction of a tenant under rent-control law.
predicates.premises_are_claimed_for_partnership_use: The premises are claimed for use by a partnership.
predicates.heir_has_no_interest_in_partnership: The heir whose requirement is relied on has no interest in the partnership.

issues.definition: If premises are claimed for partnership use in a rent-control eviction proceeding and the heir relied on has no interest in that partnership, that heir does not establish personal requirement.

issues.legal_issue: A party cannot rely on an earlier eviction decree as an existing decree unaffected by the landlord’s death when that decree was set aside and the matter remanded before the later proceedings.
material_facts: A trial court had passed a partial eviction decree during the original landlord’s lifetime.
The High Court later set aside that decree and remanded the matter for a fresh decision, including consideration of the substituted heirs’ requirement.
The appellants argued that the earlier decree could not be disturbed after the landlord’s death.
issues.conclusion: The argument was rejected because the earlier decree had been set aside and the matter remanded, so no decree remained in existence to attract the asserted exception. The court expressed no final opinion on whether an extant decree passed before a landlord’s death could be disturbed on that death.
issues.legal_principle: The court distinguished the asserted exception discussed in Phul Rani & Ors. v. Naubat Rai Ahluwalia, noting that no final opinion had been expressed there on the question. In this case, the prior decree had been set aside and the matter remanded, leaving no existing decree to which the exception could apply.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_appeal_or_revision: The proceeding is an appeal or revision arising from a rent-control eviction claim.
predicates.landlord_dies_during_proceedings: The landlord dies while the appellate or revisional proceedings are ongoing.
predicates.earlier_eviction_decree_was_set_aside_an: An earlier eviction decree was set aside and the matter was remanded before the later proceedings.

issues.definition: Where a landlord dies during an eviction appeal or revision and an earlier decree has already been set aside with the matter remanded, that decree cannot be treated as still existing.
